The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic. It's mostly apologies I don't know how to phrase, explanations that feel too late, and one message to my grandmother that I started three years ago and never finished because I couldn't decide whether to tell her I was sad or just say I loved her. I chose neither. The draft sits there, a small monument to my own cowardice.

We talk so much about the things we say. The speeches, the declarations, the carefully worded texts we agonize over before hitting send. But I've been thinking about the architecture of silence. How it holds weight. How it can be a kindness or a cruelty depending on which side of it you're standing on.

My father died when I was twenty-three. I remember the phone call, the way my mother's voice broke across the distance, the particular silence that followed when I realized that some silences are not empty but full of everything you cannot yet name. I didn't cry for three days. I kept waiting for the grief to arrive like a train, something you could hear coming. Instead it came in fragments—a song on the radio, the smell of his cologne on a stranger in an elevator, the particular way light hits a kitchen floor at 4 PM in October.

I think about how we are all, always, translating ourselves. Taking the messy interior of our minds and pressing it into language, knowing it will never quite fit. The Japanese have a word, *mono no aware*—the pathos of things, the gentle sadness of impermanence. I feel it constantly. In the way my coffee goes cold. In the way my dog's fur has started to gray around her muzzle. In the way I can remember my father's laugh but not, anymore, the exact shape of his hands.

There's a theory that we are all writing our own autobiographies in real time, that memory is not a recording but a continuous revision. I find this both comforting and terrifying. Comforting because it means we can edit, can reframe, can find new meanings in old wounds. Terrifying because it means the past is never fixed, never truly *ours*, always subject to the unreliable narrator of our present selves.

I went to a party last week and stood in the kitchen for forty minutes talking to a woman I'd just met about sourdough starters. We were both pretending. She was pretending to be interested in my fermentation process; I was pretending not to notice that her eyes kept drifting to the door. We were both waiting for something—an interruption, a rescue, a reason to leave. The sourdough was our alibi, our shared fiction that allowed us to stand close without acknowledging why we needed to.

I think about this often: how much of human connection is performance, how much is the genuine collision of two inner lives. The philosopher Martin Buber wrote about "I-Thou" relationships, moments when we truly *meet* another person, when the barriers fall away. I've had maybe a dozen of these in my life. They are rare and precious and impossible to manufacture. Most of our interactions are "I-It"—we treat each other as objects to be used, obstacles to be navigated, mirrors to reflect our own needs back at us.

The internet has made this worse and better. Worse because we can now curate our personas with surgical precision, presenting only the sourdough starter version of ourselves, the version that has their life together. Better because we can find our people—the other weirdos who also lie awake at 3 AM wondering if they're doing this right, who also keep folders of unsent messages, who also feel the weight of all the things they cannot say.

I'm thirty-four now. I used to think that by this age I would have figured something out. A career path, a sense of purpose, the ability to comfort others without needing comfort myself. Instead I have a growing collection of small wisdoms and a persistent sense that I'm still learning how to be a person. The wisdoms are things like: nobody is thinking about you as much as you think they are. And: the people who matter will wait for you to be ready. And: you can love someone and still need to leave. And: grief doesn't end, it just becomes part of the landscape.

I don't know where this is going. That's the point, I suppose. I'm writing without a destination, letting the words find their own shape. There's a kind of freedom in that, a surrender to the process. I used to outline everything, plan every paragraph, know exactly where I was going before I started. Now I'm trying to trust that if I show up honestly, something true will emerge.

My grandmother is eighty-nine. I call her every Sunday. We talk about the weather, about what she's reading, about the neighbors. We don't talk about the things that matter—her fear of dying, my fear of losing her, the way time is running out for both of us. We circle these subjects like cats circling a sleeping dog, aware of the danger but unable to approach directly. I think sometimes that love is mostly this: the courage to keep showing up, to keep making the small talk, to trust that the real conversation will happen in its own time or not at all.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver that I return to: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" I used to find this question terrifying. Now I find it tender. The wildness is still there, I think. The preciousness too. I'm just learning to be less afraid of wasting it.

I have 1000 words, the prompt said. I've used maybe 700. The rest will be silence, or the space between thoughts, or the things I'm not brave enough to write down. That's okay. Not everything needs to be said. Some things need only to be known, privately, in the dark of your own mind, where no one can judge or misunderstand or ask you to explain.

I'm going to go make some coffee now. It will probably go cold before I finish it. That's fine. That's the pathos of things. That's the wild and precious life, still unfolding, still surprising me, still mine to waste or to spend as I choose.
